The Chief Engineer (RHD) Sarak Bhaban, Dhaka ------ Appellant
Vs.

full_judgment:
Md. Iftikhar Rasool, J: This appeal at the instance of the Chief Engineer, Roads & Highways Department, Dhaka is directed against the judgment and order dated 3.7.95 passed by Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 under section 17 read with section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act making the award of the Arbitrator a Rule of the Court. 

 2. Facts giving rise to this appeal are in brief that the petitioner—respondent is a Private Limited company having expertise in the construction of Bridges and Roads throughout the country. The petitioner—respondent was adjudged as the lowest bidder in the Tender Notice No. 7-DDL/1989--90 dated 19.10.89 invited by the Executive Engineer, Roads & Highways Department, Development Division Naogaon for the construction of 155.48 meter Span prestressed Concrete Girdeer Bridge on bored Pile and well foundation over the river Atrai at Manda on the Rajshahi-Nawhata-Monhadevpur Road during the period of 1989-90. The opposite party No. 2 (who is not party in this appeal), Executive Engineer, Roads & Highways Department, Naogaon, Road Division issued the work order and accordingly the petitioner-respondent took the work and completed the same. The petitioner-respondent had done some additional works at the order of the authority. The petitioner-respondent submitted Bills for the addition works and also claimed excess price for the items which were beyond the stipulated rates. On the prayer of the respondent the opposite party-appellant appointed the Superintending Engineer, Roads & Highways Department, Planning, Monitoring & Evaluation Circle, Sarak Bhavan, Ramna, Dhaka as arbitrator for resolution of the disputes that arose between the parties and accordingly the Arbitrator gave his award on 14.12.93 after elaborate discussion but the Executive Engineer concerned did not implement the award. The Secretary, Ministry of Communication directed the opposite party-appellant to implement the award. The construction of the Bridge in question was completed in full by the end of June, 1994. The petitioner-respondent submitted a Bill of Tk. 62,16,488.45 as per the terms and conditions of the award but no positive action was taken for implementation of the award and for making payment of the amount claimed by the respondent. The petitioner-respondent was obliged to file Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 in the 1st Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for making the award a Rule of the Court. In the aforesaid Miscellaneous case the opposite party appellant entered appearance and filed written objection against the application filed by the respondent under section 17 and section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 (hereinafter referred to as the Arbitration Act contending inter alia, that the award was made beyond the statutory period of 4 (four) months and that no definite amount of money was awarded by the Arbitrator. The Arbitrator misconducted himself in awarding increased rates in violation of the terms and conditions of the tender and contract. It is stated by the opposite party appellant in the written objection that the Arbitrator misconducted in making the award only m the basis of discussions and relying upon the letters of the petitioner-Respondent and as such the award so made by the Arbitrator is liable to be set aside. 

 5. It appears that Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 was initiated by the petitioner respondent under section 17 read with section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act for making the award a Rule of the Court. In the above Miscellaneous case the arbitrator was made opposite party No.1. 

 6. The learned Deputy Attorney General Mr. Altaf Hossain Khan submits that the Arbitrator made delay in making the award and as such the award given by him long after the period of 4(four) months is hit by Article 3 of the First Schedule to the Arbitration Act. According to him the award given by the Arbitrator beyond the statutory period of 4(four) months the same is not an award in the eye of law, it having been barred by limitation. The next plea raised by the learned Deputy General is that the award ought to have been filed in Court within 90(ninety) days for making the award a Rule or the court and failure to so the period of limitation as laid down in Article 178 of the Limitation Act will come into play and in this view of the matter the award having been filed long after the period of 90 (ninety) days it cannot legally be made a Rule of the Court. It is further submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Subordinate Judge missed this vital point of law of limitation while making the award a Rule of the Court by the impugned order. It is further urged by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Subordinate Judge while making the award a Rule of the Court he failed to consider vital question of misconduct on the party of the Arbitrator in making the award which plea was forcefully taken by the opposite party-appellant in his written objection filed under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. It is further argued by him that the Subordinate Judge omitted to make mention of this plea in the impugned order. It is further submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Arbitrator went out of his way to refer to the letters as placed before him by the petitioner-respondent taking the same as unquestionable pieces of evidence for fixing the, rates commensurate with the claims made by the respondent and he did not discuss in detail the reasons for his acceptance of the letters of the petitioner —respondent. It is argued by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Arbitrator misconducted in giving the award almost in such a manner as if no one opposed the claim or claims of the petitioner-respondent. In Clause 25 of the General Rules for the guidance of the contractors it has been clearly provided that the Arbitrator shall make such enquiry or investigation as he deems fit and proper to arrive at a decision but in this case he made a clear departure from the provisions laid down in Clause 25 of the aforesaid General Rules. He simply conducted the proceedings in his own way without considering the case of the other side. There were 11 items which were the bones of contention between the parties. While making the award the Arbitrator did only the desk work and gave award in arbitrary manner which amounted to misconduct. It was incumbent upon the Arbitrator to visit the site for ascertaining the truth or otherwise of the claims of the petitioner respondent. The failure of the Arbitrator to visit the site of the works speaks volume of his misconduct. It is further asserted by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the Subordinate Judge signally failed to notice the misconduct of the arbitrator which on the face of them are very much clear and these therefore, had cut at the root of the award that he gave. 

 7. Mr. Mohammad Habibullah, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner-respondent submits that the point raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General on the question of limitation for making the award as envisaged in Article 3 of the 1st schedule to the Arbitration Act has been set at rest by a decision reported in the case in the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Director of Movement & Storage Department Vs. Jalaluddin Ahmed reported in 37 D.L.R. (AD) 27. The learned Counsel for the petitioner-respondent contends that in the above decision it has been held that in an arbitration proceedings if any party raises no objection regarding continuation of the proceedings beyond 4 (four) months as per the provisions of Article 3 of the first schedule to the Arbitration Act, such party will be deemed to have waived its right to raise the plea of limitation as enjoined in the above article, Turning to the question of limitation in filing application for making the award a Rule of the Court, he submits that the period of 90 (ninety) days provided in Article 178 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application to the facts and circumstances of the instant case. He submits that as both the parties were present in the Arbitration proceedings from the very beginning there was no necessity for service of notice under section 14(1) of the Arbitration Act. So, according to him, in view of the presence of both the parties in the proceedings the period for filing application in Court for making the award a Rule of the Court will be three years as per Article 181 of the Limitation Act & this period will be computed from the date of making the award. It is submitted by him further that the award in this case was made on 14.12.1993 and the petitioner/respondent started the Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 for the purpose of making the award a Rule of the Court on 8.3.95 and this date is well within the time-frame as laid down in Article 181 of the Limitation Act. In support of his above contention the learned Counsel for the petitioner respondent has referred to the citation reported in 41 D.L.R. 504 in the case of Bajia Rice Mills Vs. Bangladesh. It is further argued by the learned lawyer for the petitioner-respondent that the opposite party-appellant was present all throughout the proceedings in the arbitration and that the plea of misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator as raised by the opposite party-appellant has no legs to stand upon. According to the learned Counsel for the petitioner/respondent, the petitioner-respondent has acquired vast-experience in the field of construction of Bridges and Roads and the question of their making inflated claim is beyond question and the Arbitrator having been fully satisfied with the genuineness of the claim of the petitioner-respondent allowed the rates for the additional works done by them and there was no scope for misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator. According to him without making a positive move by the appellant he cannot hope to set the award aside. In this connection he has referred to a decision reported in 43 D.L.R. (AD) 217 in the case of Bangladesh & others Vs. K.M. Shafi Ltd. It is further argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioner-respondent that the opposite party-appellant cannot legally maintain the appeal for not taking a definite plea for setting aside the award either under section 17 or under section 33 of the Arbitration Act before the Court having jurisdiction and as such the appeal so preferred by the opposite party-appellant is utterly a misconceived one. While making this submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner-respondent has drawn our attention to the memorandum of appeal which has not been filed with-out mentioning any section of the Arbitration Act and he sum up by saying that the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 9. The time limit for giving the award by the Arbitrator has been discussed at length in case of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Director of Movement and Storage, Department of Food Vs. Jalaluddin Ahmed as reported in 37 D.L.R (A.D) 27. It has been held in the aforesaid decision that when an arbitration proceedings are continued beyond 4(four) months with either party raising no objection regarding such continuation the conclusion is that the party concerned has waived its right, with regard to the question of limitation as laid down in Article 3 of the 1st schedule to the Arbitration Act. This decision sets at rest the plea of limitation as raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General on this point. The next question on the point of limitation raised by the learned Deputy Attorney General is with regard to the time limit, which according to him, is 90 (ninety) days for filing an application before the appropriate court for making the award a Rule of the Court and this limitation will be governed by An Article 178 of the Limitation Act. To appreciate the correct position of law we are to consider sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 14 of the Arbitration Act. Sub-sections (1) and (2) are as under:- 

 10. Sub-section (1) of section 14 clearly lays down that after making an award by the Arbitrator he shall sign the award and give notice in writing to the parties informing of the fact of making and signing of the award. Sub-section (2) provides for filing the award by the Arbitrator suo moto in Court for making the award a Rule of the Court and this sub-section also provides for filing an application before the appropriate Court praying for directing the Arbitrator to file the award in Court for making .the award a Rule of the Court. The Court concerned shall direct the Arbitrator to file the award in Court and also shall give notice to the parties as to the filing of the award in the Court. Sub-section (2) of section 14 does not provide for any time limit to give direction to the arbitrator to file the award in Court. In the instant case as both the parties were present all throughout the proceedings till making of the award, and signing of it by the arbitrator, there is no necessity of giving notice by the Arbitrator to the parties as to the making of the award or signing of it. The question of limitation as envisaged under Article 178 of the Limitation Act has therefore, no manner of application in this case and the limitation of 3(three) years as provided for in Article 181 of the Limitation Act will be applicable and this period of limitation will run from making of the award i.e. on and from 24.12.1993. The petitioner-respondent appears to have filed Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 on 8.3.95 which date is well within the period of limitation as provided for in Article 181 of the Limitation. Act and as such we are of the view that the Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 is not barred by limitation. This view taken by us is in line with the decision reported in 41 D.L.R. 504 as mentioned by us herein before. We will come to consider the question of misconduct of the Arbitrator later after we have considered the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioner-respondent that the opposite party appellant cannot maintain this appeal when he independently has failed to make a positive move for setting aside the award either under section 17 or under section 33 of the Arbitration Act. 

 11. On perusal of the application of Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 it appears that the petitioner-respondent has filed the above miscellaneous case under section 17 read with section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act. Section 17 of the Arbitration Act reads as follows: 

 (a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings; 

 13. Now let us turn to the allegations of misconduct of the Arbitrator as raised by the opposite party appellant. We have already mentioned some aspects of the Clause 25 of the General Rules for the guidance of the contractors. We have in a nutshell pointed out the functions and the manner in which the Arbitrator has to discharge his liabilities. His position is a position of trust. In the instant case the arbitrator appears to have relied upon the letters and correspondence of the respondent in allowing them the rates as claimed by them for the additional works and excess materials they alleged to have used and these are matters required for closed physical verification upon visit of the works by the Arbitrator. There were 11 items regarding which the disputes between the parties centre round. There were no materials before the Arbitrator on the basis of which he determined the rates in favour of the respondent except the letters and correspondence which the respondent produced before the Arbitrator at the time of the arbitration proceedings and the Arbitrator made a subjective calculation of the rates without advancing any convincing reasons for his so doing. Without physical verification of the alleged additional works done and excess materials used by the respondent upon a visit to the site of the works by the Arbitrator, the calculation of the rates worked out by the arbitrator sitting at his desk lacked objectivity which is indicative of misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator. The Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka seems to have completely over-looked this very important question of misconduct on the part of the Arbitrator giving the award and as such he committed illegality in making the award a Rule of the Court by the impugned Judgment and order. In the circumstances and for the reasons stated above we are inclined to allow the appeal. 

 14. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned Judgment and order passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka on 03.07.1995 in Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1995 is hereby set aside.
